title: Neena Gupta, Who Answered a 70-Year-Old Maths Problem, Named to TIME100 Next India
excerpt: The ISI Kolkata professor found a counterexample to the Zariski Cancellation Problem in 2014. TIME's new India list puts her among its Health and Science Innovators.
body:
• Neena Gupta, a professor at the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata, has been named to the TIME100 Next India 2026 list in its Health and Science Innovators category.
  • In 2014 she found a counterexample to a version of the Zariski Cancellation Problem, a question in algebraic geometry first posed by Oscar Zariski in 1949.
  • Her honours include the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in 2019, the Ramanujan Prize in 2021 and the Infosys Prize in Mathematical Sciences in 2024.
  • Gupta completed her mathematics honours degree at Bethune College in 2006 and her PhD at ISI Kolkata in 2011, and has spent her research career there.

Neena Gupta, a professor in the Theoretical Statistics and Mathematics Unit at the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI) in Kolkata, has been named in TIME100 Next India 2026, in the list's Health and Science Innovators category. The list recognises emerging leaders whose work is shaping India's future, according to coverage of the announcement. Gupta's place on it rests on a result she produced more than a decade ago, in one of the most abstract corners of mathematics.

The problem she answered

The Zariski Cancellation Problem, posed by Oscar Zariski in 1949, belongs to algebraic geometry. In plain terms, it asks whether two mathematical structures that become equivalent after an extra dimension is added must also have been equivalent in their original form. For nearly seven decades, the question went unanswered.

In 2014, Gupta showed that the assumption does not always hold. Using a three-dimensional affine variety constructed by the mathematician Takanori Asanuma, she established a counterexample in positive characteristic: two structures can become equivalent once a dimension is added even when their original structures are not equivalent. The Government of India's Department of Science and Technology has described her work as a solution to the longstanding problem, and it brought her research in algebraic geometry into the international spotlight.

From Kolkata classrooms to ISI

Gupta was born in Kolkata in 1984. She completed her Bachelor of Science (Honours) in Mathematics at Bethune College in 2006, then joined ISI Kolkata, where she completed her master's degree in 2008 and her PhD in 2011, specialising in algebra under Professor Amartya Kumar Dutta, according to Jagran's profile. She returned to ISI to build her research and teaching career there. Gupta has spoken about being the only woman in her postgraduate mathematics class, an experience that underlined the gender imbalance in the discipline.

A decade of honours

The 2014 result began a run of recognition. Gupta received the Indian National Science Academy's Young Scientist Award in 2014 and the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Mathematical Sciences in 2019, one of India's highest scientific honours. In 2021 she became the third woman to receive the Ramanujan Prize, awarded for her work in affine algebraic geometry and commutative algebra. She was conferred the Nari Shakti Puraskar in March 2022, and in 2024 she received the Infosys Prize in Mathematical Sciences for her work on the Zariski Cancellation Problem. In 2025, she delivered the 44th Emmy Noether Lecture, organised by the Association for Women in Mathematics and the American Mathematical Society.

Why it matters

Gupta's inclusion in TIME100 Next India 2026 adds a pure mathematician to a list dominated by founders, policymakers and public figures. Her result did not produce a product or a policy; it settled, for an important class of cases, a question about how mathematical structures behave — the kind of foundational answer that other researchers build on for decades. For students in India considering research mathematics, her career also offers a concrete path: educated entirely in Kolkata, at Bethune College and ISI, and recognised internationally without leaving either institution.
